speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: asked the Minister for National Development to encourage marriage and parenthood, whether the Government will consider (i) advance construction of more HDB BTO projects to shorten the waiting period of first-time applicants and (ii) extension of the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme to couples awaiting their BTO flats and whose household income is between $7,000 and $14,000, instead of only to those earning $7,000 and below.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: asked the Minister for National Development what specific measures can the Government implement to shorten the waiting time for new HDB BTO projects to less than three years going forward.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is achieved by bringing forward the construction works for specific sites that are ready for development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The pipeline of shorter waiting time flats has been impacted during the pandemic due to construction delays and disruptions as well as higher BTO demand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where possible, we also endeavour to launch more BTO projects with shorter waiting times, subject to site and infrastructure readiness.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While waiting for the completion of their new flats, most flat buyers continue to stay with family members or relatives, or rent on the open market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS) provides an additional temporary housing option for eligible households.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The income ceiling of $7,000 is pegged to the typical income ceiling for 3-room BTO flats in the non-mature estates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is also well above the median monthly household income of PPHS applicants, which was $5,700 before the income ceiling was introduced and $4,400 in the past year since the income ceiling was put in place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While we are on track to double the supply of interim flats for PPHS between 2021 and 2023, the supply remains limited.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As such, we will retain the income ceiling so as to continue prioritising those who are less able to afford renting on the open market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Households whose incomes exceed the $7,000 ceiling but who need help with temporary housing due to exceptional circumstances, such as high medical expenses or other needs, may approach HDB.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: HDB will consider their requests on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My questions are directed towards promoting the national objective of marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Would MND consider, one, a different type of BTO, a "Build-then-Order", instead of Build-to-Order scheme, so that flats can be built in advance for registered married couples, for example, applying for the first time, in order to encourage marriage and parenthood?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I know that building in advance creates stock inventory and it might be costly, but if we could ringfence this for marriage and parenthood, on which the nation is already spending quite a bit of money, it might be well worth it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My second supplementary question is whether the Minister would consider helping young couples beyond the "between $7,000 and $14,000" bracket, which is the eligibility for applying BTO flats, to help them get a rental flat on an interim basis.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is, again, based on what we know about the market that many young couples are renting flats before they get their BTOs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If they live with their parents, they might also be delaying parenthood.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, again, all the questions are directed towards promoting marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, I have just described the shorter waiting time model which has been in place since 2018, where we launch construction and then launch the project.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, as a result, applicants can get their flat under three years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The construction disruptions and delays during COVID-19 had affected some of that pipeline.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That is something we are committed to do.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But in addition to that, we have the Sale of Balance Flats exercise and the Open Booking of Flats exercise by HDB, and, of course, resale flats, which are available with grants for eligible buyers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And at this point in time, while resale prices have gone up, with measures to moderate demand, we hope to manage the price increases in the resale market as well to ensure affordability for first-time home buyers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As for the Member's request to raise or remove the income ceiling for PPHS, I have explained earlier why we need to maintain this for the time being.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Demand has been high, particularly because of the construction delays caused by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have been using some of the SERS units, some of the unsold units, we have also taken some rental flats – and you see there is a trade-off there – we have also taken over staff apartments from the Polytechnics and repurposed them for PPHS during this period.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, to provide support for those who may have even greater difficulty affording rental in the interim, we maintain the income ceiling as well as the priority for married couples with children below the age of 18.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Minister just alluded to HDB's attempt to complete within three years.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Can the Minister give some guidance exactly what percentage of future launches will likely fall within the three-year timeframe, just so to give us a guidance?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: HDB's mission remains the same even through COVID-19 and even as we continue to deal with the after-effects on the construction sector and on development of properties in general arising from the last two years' pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, to ensure affordability and accessibility, we have been doing a couple of things.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have also put in property cooling measures to moderate demand in the resale market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Lastly, of course, is tackling the issue of construction delays.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: HDB has been working very closely with the contractors and their supply chain to manage overall construction delays and there has been progress made on that front.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We need to expedite construction, but will do so safely and without compromising the quality of flats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, in the last two years, HDB and all developers and contractors have been affected by supply chain disruptions because a lot of materials come from abroad – construction material, parts and even manpower to help us construct.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And during the pandemic and emerging from COVID-19, HDB continues to work very closely with our contractors, helping them to obtain the manpower that is necessary, helping them to stabilise prices of steel and concrete through HDB's schemes to support the contractors, and working very hard with our local supply chain to ensure greater domestic resilience, whether by stockpiling offsite, stockpiling in Singapore or working more closely with our prefabrication plants to have the capability to churn out more components for HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Through standardisation and good design, we can achieve that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Recently, in the HDB awards, I announced more efforts by HDB to try out new methods of construction that will allow it to drive even greater productivity and, hence, be more resilient to supply chain disruptions that may come in the future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As for the Member's question about the percentage of shorter waiting times for flats, as I have said earlier, we have delivered 7,200 over the last two years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There has been an impact because BTO demand has been high and also because there have been disruptions to construction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we work hard to raise the quantum of shorter waiting time flats even as we continue to grapple with the after-effects of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Minister mentioned that the supply is still quite tight.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Government's decision to double the PPHS units is most welcomed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My question is in relation to the number of applicants who satisfy the current criterion of salary ceiling of $7,000 or below.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How many people who satisfy the salary ceiling still cannot get the PPHS units and what options are there for them?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I had, in my Question No 38 set down in the Order Paper for today, made two suggestions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One is in relation to support for applicants who cannot rely on their families to get rental flats from the public rental market.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The other one is in relation to some form of grant to enable them to get the rental flat on their own.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think the Member has asked a question which is actually further down the line.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But, since he has already asked it, I am just wondering whether to wait till then or give him a sneak peek into the answer I am going to give him.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Both prior to the imposition of the income ceiling and the other measures and, even now, with the measures in place, on average, we see about 47% of PPHS applicants who decided not to make a selection when they are invited to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But, of course, that means others further down the queue will then be invited and that ensures that the flats are occupied.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One suggestion I had previously made was to look at the supply of resale flats and how we can have more of that in the market because, with more resale flats in the market, that would lower the retail price and, hopefully, get more first-timers looking to the resale market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And the suggestion I previously made was to look at reducing or waiving the Minimum Occupation Period (MOP) period for resale flats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To be fair, I think the answer I was given then was that that may not be a viable solution because those who sell resale flats will go back into the market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, would the Minister consider waiving or reducing the MOP for those who sell resale flats but do not intend to go back into the market, say, for those who are moving to stay with their children or maybe even upgrading to private property?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The MOP is intended to reinforce the owner occupation intent for public housing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Whether it is five or 10 years or somewhere in between, we have to strike a balance because, ultimately, there is a minimum period where you need to occupy your flats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With children on the way, they may need more space, they may need to move closer to a school or they may have other arrangements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, when people need to sell their flats within MOP, generally, we do not waive, but we do look at individual requests on a case-by-case basis to understand the circumstances they face in deciding whether to grant the waiver of MOP or not.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And, in fact, that will, in a way, serve to cater to the groups of people who need to move during that period.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But whether we will do so in order to increase the supply of resale flats in the market, I am not quite so sure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When you shorten the MOP, you may see that there will then be demand in other parts of the market.
